sources.title: Kazi Nazrul Islam (Q334818), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Kazi Nazrul Islam', description 'National poet of Bangladesh', Bengali label কাজী নজরুল ইসলাম, Korean label 카지 나즈룰 이슬람 (Korean Wikipedia article of the same title), instance of human, born 24 May 1899, died 29 August 1976, citizenship claims for British India, India and Bangladesh. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Rafiqul Islam, 'Islam, Kazi Nazrul', Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh; entry read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the 'rebel poet' and national poet of Bangladesh who used subjects and vocabulary new to Bangla poetry, whose poems 'Vidrohi' and 'Bhangar Gan' (written 1921) and the collection Agni-Vina (1922) changed the tenor of Bangla poetry, who founded the paper Dhumketu in August 1922, was jailed in 1923 after a proscribed poem and held a 40-day hunger strike, edited Langal and helped organise the Sramik Praja Swaraj Dal in 1925-26, was mainly the creator of the Bangla ghazal and composed some two thousand songs, worked for HMV, radio, stage and film, and from 1942 lived the rest of his life in silence. Detailed, dated, largely admiring reference entry that also records conservative Muslim and Hindu criticism of him and his 1923 and 1930 prosecutions.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kazi Nazrul Islam' (read). Independent reference biography: born 1899, father's death in 1908 and his work as caretaker of a mausoleum, the folk-theatre troupe, cook and tea-stall jobs, enlisting in 1917, his literary circle in Calcutta, the poem 'Bidrohi' of 1922 as his most famous work, his arrest in January 1923 over 'Anondomoyeer Agomone' and a 40-day prison fast, protest songs such as 'Karar Oi Louho Kopat', the HMV association from 1928 to 1932, songs for film and radio so that his musical career 'gradually eclipsed his political activities', and the later move to Dhaka and burial at the University of Dhaka. Short reference article; the totals of his songs are given as a range of 2,000 to 4,000.

Basanti (Calcutta illustrated weekly), vol. 1, part 4, issues 37-47, April-June 1923, scan from the University of Calcutta's copy in the Digital Library of India collection on the Internet Archive (scanned pages and OCR text; the editorial notes of issue 42, 19 May 1923, and issue 44, and the poem 'Kono ek kabir prati' with Nazrul's captioned photograph in issue 47 were read in Bengali). CONTEMPORARY NON-SELF SOURCE: while he was fasting in Hooghly jail the editor wrote that the young rebel poet was courting death by hunger, that more than a month had passed, and that some might call him capricious and others foolish; a later note says that after thirty-eight days he took food at the request of the older woman Biraja Sundari Devi; another note reports that the press and his friends were refused permission to visit him. Sympathetic weekly; the dates and day-count differ slightly from Banglapedia.

MD Shahnawaz Khan Chandan, 'The Life of a Rebel', The Daily Star, Dhaka (29 August 2013; read in full). Tribute article: his jobs as a mosque imam, bakery worker and cook, enlisting in the army, founding Nabayug with Muzaffar Ahmed in 1920, the 1922 magazine Dhumketu and the poem that led to his arrest, the 40-day fast, the 1930 sedition conviction, his marriage to Pramila Devi and the criticism it drew, his film Dhruva Bhakta (1934) as director, composer and actor, and the Vienna treatment. Admiring and anecdotal (it includes an unsourced taxi story and says he never wrote for money, which this profile does not use); it says he enlisted partly as a protest at the belief that Bengalis were unfit for war, a motive Banglapedia does not give.

'Nazrul: Bengal's Beloved Rebel Poet', Live History India (read in full). Popular history article: his travelling-theatre start, army years and reading of Hafiz, Rumi and Khayyam, the poems 'Bidrohi' and 'Bhangar Gaan', Dhumketu and Tagore's blessing, the 1923 arrest and fast, his criticism of both the Khilafat movement and the Congress's hesitation over independence, his help in organising the Sramik Praja Swaraj Dal, his marriage to Pramila Devi and its criticism, and his songs and children's verse. Celebratory; follows the same record as the encyclopedias and gives no new documents.

Arka Deb, 'Forbidden Nazrul', The Daily Star (31 August 2025; read in full). Essay on literary censorship: at least five of his books were banned (Yugavani 1922, Bhangar Gan 1924, Bisher Banshi 1924, Pralay Shikha and Chandrabindu 1931), police seized 350 copies of Yugavani from the publisher and he listed himself as its publisher to shield the publishing house, the collection's essays on trade and servitude, and the long afterlife of the song 'Karar Oi Louho Kopat'. Interpretive and admiring, with comparisons to Voltaire and Solzhenitsyn; used here only for the bans and the publisher detail.

Mohammad Rahmatullah and Tanu Gupta, 'Kazi Nazrul Islam's Poetry and the Affairs of Contemporary Life', Literature & Aesthetics 32(1), 2022 (University of Sydney open journal; peer-reviewed essay; the abstract, introduction and sampled sections were read from the open-access PDF). Literary-critical reading of 'The Rebel' and other poems in the light of Michael Oakeshott's view of poetry, arguing that his 'I' becomes a universal voice for the oppressed and that his poems call for equality across Hindu, Buddhist, Muslim and Christian. Independent scholarly view of the poems' meaning; not behavioural evidence and not used for any row.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_basanti, src_nazrul_forbidden, src_nazrul_britannica | 1922-1931 | reference encyclopedia, contemporary weekly, essay, reference encyclopedia] After his poem 'Anandamayir Agamane' appeared in his own paper Dhumketu in September 1922 the issue was proscribed, his essay book Yugavani was banned on 23 November 1922 and he was arrested the same day; he gave a written deposition in his own defence in January 1923 (acknowledged as literature) and was sentenced to a year's rigorous imprisonment. In Hooghly jail from 14 April 1923 he began a hunger strike against the ill-treatment of political prisoners, which Banglapedia gives as 40 days and the contemporary weekly Basanti as 38, and which Banglapedia says ended after the prison inspector's persuasion and the weekly says ended at the request of an older woman, Biraja Sundari Devi; Basanti's editor, writing during the fast, said some might call it caprice and others folly. Banglapedia adds a second conviction in 1930 (dropped in 1931 under the Gandhi-Irwin pact), and Arka Deb counts at least five banned books between 1922 and 1931 and notes that he listed himself as the publisher of Yugavani. The arrest and fast are documented by a contemporaneous source as well as by reference works, and the cost to him (prison, bans) was real. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 82 / 0.70 to 78 / 0.66 because the arrest and fast are retold across reference works, the contemporary notes confirm only the fast and the arrest, and the 1930 case rests on one entry.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_lhi | 1921-1926 | reference encyclopedia, history magazine] Banglapedia says he did not imitate any poet, not even Tagore, though imitation was the fashion, and that in 1921 he had no faith in the philosophy of Gandhi's non-cooperation movement or of the Khilafat movement, believed only armed revolution would free India and backed Mustafa Kemal's Turkey (the poem 'Kamal Pasha'), yet joined the processions for the sake of a united anti-imperial struggle; Live History India says he was as critical of the Khilafat movement's 'hollow religious fundamentalism' as of the Congress's hesitation over full independence while still joining the Bengal Congress and helping organise the Sramik Praja Swaraj Dal. The two accounts follow the same record and describe his views rather than show them in separate dated episodes. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.56 because the second source repeats the first and the Khilafat poem is described, not quoted.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_britannica, src_nazrul_forbidden | 1921-1928 | reference encyclopedia, reference encyclopedia, essay] Banglapedia says he used subjects and vocabulary never used in Bangla poetry before, drew on Sanskrit and Arabic metres and Persian and Hindu archetypes, that 'Vidrohi' and 'Bhangar Gan' changed the tenor of Bangla poetry and that Agni-Vina, whose first edition sold out soon after publication, was a turning point; it says the Bangla ghazal is mainly his creation. Britannica calls 'Bidrohi' his most famous work, and Arka Deb says the editorials of Yugavani remain unusually fresh. These are the judgments of encyclopedias and a later essayist rather than documented episodes of how he worked. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.66 to 76 / 0.60 because the claims of newness come from one encyclopedia entry. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered again to 74 / 0.58 because the evidence is critical reception and praise, not behaviour.

experimentation.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_britannica | 1927-1942 | reference encyclopedia, reference encyclopedia] Banglapedia says that at Krishnanagar he composed ghazals built like Urdu ones, which became the Bangla ghazal, set songs to notation, wrote for the gramophone, acted in, directed and composed for the 1934 film Bhakta Dhruva (17 of its 18 songs) and worked on later films, and from 1939 to 1942 made raga-based radio programmes of exceptional quality; Britannica describes songs blending folk, classical and devotional traditions. The trials of new forms are documented, but by two reference works in summary form and without his own account of testing and revising. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.50 because the sources list new forms without showing iteration.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_britannica, src_nazrul_dailystar_life | 1919-1945 | reference encyclopedia, reference encyclopedia, tribute article] Banglapedia documents sustained work in poetry, short stories and novels, journalism (Nabajug, Dhumketu, Langal), party organising, song composition with notation, gramophone and radio work, songs for about twenty stage plays, film acting and direction, and translations of Hafiz and Omar Khayyam; Britannica and the Daily Star describe the same breadth. The breadth is documented across many fields, but it is partly the output record. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.58 because several of the fields are counted from a list of works rather than from separate episodes.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_lhi, src_nazrul_dailystar_life | 1920-1926 | reference encyclopedia, history magazine, tribute article] He ran the evening daily Nabajug from July 1920 (Banglapedia says Fazlul Huq was the named editor but Nazrul did most of the work; the Daily Star says he started it with Muzaffar Ahmed), launched Dhumketu in August 1922, edited the weekly Langal from December 1925 as chief editor, helped organise the Sramik Praja Swaraj Dal and in November 1926 stood for a seat in the upper house of the central legislative council. The papers and the party were joint efforts and the outcomes (the paper's deposit forfeited, the party short-lived) are not assessed. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.52 because each venture was shared with others and the sources do not say who initiated what.

adaptability.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_dailystar_life | 1908-1920 | reference encyclopedia, tribute article] After his father's death in 1908 he took over as caretaker and muezzin, left to join a travelling folk-theatre troupe (writing its plays and songs), returned to school, worked as a cook and at a tea stall, went back to school, enlisted in 1917, rose to havildar, and after leaving the army in 1920 began a new life as a journalist in Calcutta. The moves are documented, but they were driven largely by poverty and family loss, and the Daily Star's claim that he enlisted as a protest is not given by Banglapedia. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.46 because the changes were forced by circumstances more than chosen.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_nazrul_banglapedia, src_nazrul_forbidden, src_nazrul_dailystar_life | 1925-1927 | reference encyclopedia, essay, tribute article] Banglapedia says that Langal was the mouthpiece of a workers' and peasants' party whose manifesto demanded full independence and aimed to end class differences, that his 1925 book Samyabadi o Sarbahara collected songs for workers and peasants and that from 1926 his patriotic songs turned to the downtrodden masses; Arka Deb quotes his editorials urging Bengalis to enter business without an inferiority complex and denouncing servitude. These show aims directed at others over several years, but they are mostly texts and one party's manifesto. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.50 because the tribute article's claim that he never wrote for money is not used and the rest rests on one entry. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered again to 64 / 0.48 because writing for a cause is shown by his texts, not by costs borne for others.

portrait.source: Photograph of Kazi Nazrul Islam, standing with folded arms, printed with the Bengali caption 'kabi kaji nazrul' (Poet Kazi Nazrul) beside the poem 'Kono ek kabir prati' (To a certain poet), which honours the poet's hunger strike in prison, in Basanti (Calcutta illustrated weekly), vol. 1, part 4, issue no. 47, 1923 (printed page 263; the weekly's issue no. 42 is dated 19 May 1923). Taken from the Internet Archive scan of the University of Calcutta's copy in the Digital Library of India collection (item dli.calcutta.00534, 913 x 1193 page image); this file is the photograph cropped from that page at the scan's own resolution, not resized and not upscaled. Photographer not named. The sitter is identified by the printed caption and the poem's content. Commons holds a separate crop of the same issue's cover portrait (Basanti, 19 May 1923, signed in facsimile); that image was not used.
portrait.license: Public domain: photograph by an unknown photographer first published in British India in 1923 (before 1931, so out of copyright in the United States); anonymous photographs published in 1923 are also out of term under Indian and Bangladeshi law (60 years from publication). The Internet Archive item has no rights field or reuse restriction; its collection notice describes non-commercial fair-dealing hosting by the library and claims no copyright
portrait.attribution: Unknown photographer, printed in Basanti (Calcutta), 1923; scan of the University of Calcutta copy, Digital Library of India, via the Internet Archive
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer (printed in Basanti)

provenance.notes: Roster70. PORTRAIT PREFLIGHT: Stage B grade PLAUSIBLE (Stage A risky); the lead (Commons 'Nazrul young in 1921.jpg', a 2021 phone photograph of an Agni-Vina print by an uploader, with 'Bishnupuri (1919)' in the author field) did NOT survive and was replaced: no scan of any Agni-Vina edition shows a portrait (the Internet Archive scan of the second edition, Sept-Oct 1923, has none), so the 1922 publication chain could not be confirmed. REPLACEMENT: the Basanti weekly, vol. 1 part 4 (Calcutta, 1923), is the very volume Commons cites for its 408 x 517 cover crop; I opened the Internet Archive scan (Digital Library of India, University of Calcutta copy, item dli.calcutta.00534), found the cover portrait of issue 42 (19 May 1923, facsimile signature, issue discusses his fast) and a second photograph with the printed caption naming him beside a poem about his hunger strike (issue 47, p. 263), and shipped the captioned photograph (376 x 492 at the scan's native resolution; the cover portrait would be larger but is identified only by a faint signature). Holder record: the IA metadata (dates, 'Bengali Journals, University of Calcutta', collection notice about non-commercial fair-dealing hosting) was read; the item has no dc.rights field (the scan of a different DLI book, Agni-Vina 2nd ed., says 'In Public Domain'); no permission, fee or reproduction restriction found. Age-only path: first published in British India in 1923 by an unknown photographer, so US public domain by pre-1931 publication and out of term in India and Bangladesh. Kind likeness. Jurisdiction-only images (Nazrul Institute 'Nazrul.jpg', 1926) were not used. IDENTITY: QID Q334818 verified live 2026-11-24 (human; Bengali label কাজী নজরুল ইসলাম; born 24 May 1899, died 29 August 1976). Region south_asia, nationality BD and IN with the British Raj polity as for Tagore; era 20th_century (career from 1919-20). Korean name 카지 나즈룰 이슬람 (Wikidata ko label and Korean Wikipedia title). EVIDENCE: attribution is attributable (dated arrests, bans, papers and prosecutions; a contemporaneous 1923 weekly confirms the fast). Eight rows; not scored on purpose: risk tolerance (considered at 68 / 0.50 and removed because it re-counted the same arrest-and-fast episodes as conflict tolerance), teamwork, staying power and social assertiveness (re-count the same episodes or lack a separate source). EXCLUDED ON PURPOSE: his illness from 1942, any diagnosis and the later suffering (private condition; the Daily Star and Live History India mention a diagnosis and the Daily Star an asylum, neither is used), marriage and family life apart from the fact of the inter-religious marriage criticism (not scored), honours, and the 'national poet' title as evidence. CONFLICTS NOT ADJUDICATED: length of the hunger strike (38, 39 or 40 days), date of the court judgment (8 or 16 January 1923; Banglapedia gives the 16th) and the date of his arrest (Banglapedia 23 Nov 1922, others January 1923), the reason he enlisted. 'The New Nation' and a political-science site were read and rejected as derivative of Wikipedia and Britannica. Not opened or blocked: Wikipedia (orientation only), the Wire article (script page), BSS (403), Daily Star 'anti-colonial essays' (paywalled).
